paper.title: Price response in residential electricity demand: Evidence from Danish smart meter data
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no DST project reference is printed. …

registers.name_in_paper: Moduldata for elmaalere (hourly smart electricity meter data, Danmarks Statistik)
registers.role: outcome and sample frame: hourly household electricity consumption C_{i,a,t}, and the deciles of total electricity consumption used as a household characteristic
variables_mentioned: C_{i,a,t}: hourly consumption of household i

registers.role: linkage: uniquely assigns electricity meters to households, and the consumption recorded to the household living at the address at a given point in time

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish registry data / Danish administrative registers (micro-data)
registers.role: sample frame and household characteristics for the heterogeneity analysis
variables_mentioned: average age of adult household members
highest educational attainment by any adult family member
whether the household operates an electric vehicle

registers.role: household characteristic: the EV-user indicator, including plug-in hybrid cars

registers.name_in_paper: Energinet: electricity spot price (eltarif), transmission grid and system tariff, local distribution grid tariff (Table A.2)
registers.role: treatment: components of the constructed hourly household price P_{i,a,t} in Eq. (2.1)
treatment: the tax component T_t of the constructed hourly price

linkages: electricity meters are linked to an address via the Danish address registry, and the recorded consumption is assigned to the household living at that address at a given point in time
each hourly consumption observation is matched to its corresponding hourly marginal price by time and geographic location (grid area)
after estimating a semi-elasticity for each household, the household-level estimates are merged with socio-demographic characteristics from the registry data for 2020
households are matched to the 2022 vehicle register ('Bilregister') to identify electric-vehicle users

sample.universe: Households with a smart electricity meter in the Radius grid area (Greater Copenhagen, price zone DK2) and the Trefor grid area (Jutland, price zone DK1); since the beginning of 2020 every Danish household is required by law to have a smart electricity meter
sample.unit_of_observation: household-hour for the elasticity estimation (Eqs. 3.3-3.4); household for the demographic regressions (Eq. 5.1 and Table A.3); hour for the first stage reported in Table 1
selection_rules: restrict the sample to households that were present in the micro-data between 2020 and 2023
only consider unique household address combinations, which excludes e.g. student accommodation or shared apartments
exclude addresses with an hourly electricity consumption registered as exactly 0 kWh for a week or more
exclude addresses that used more than 25 kWh within an hour for more than 1000 h throughout the full sample
exclude households with an extremely high or low total consumption: the top and bottom 1/75 of the sample by total consumption
for computational reasons the analysis is performed only for a subsample of households from the Radius and Trefor grid areas
Table 2 and Fig. 2 trim the top and bottom 1% of the estimated semi-elasticities
the demographic regressions keep households that can be matched to the registry variables used in the column
sample.n_observations: 30 644 hourly observations per grid area in the first stage (Table 1)
sample.n_individuals: a subset of almost 25,000 households; 24 395 households with an estimated semi-elasticity after trimming (12 609 Radius, 11 786 Trefor); 23 597-24 050 in the Table 3 regressions and 23 664-24 131 in the Table A.3 probits

construction_notes: the household-specific price is constructed as in Eq. (2.1): P_{i,a,t} = (1+tau)[E_{i,a,t} + G^T_t + G^D_{a,t} + T_t], with VAT tau = 0.25

because provider-specific markups over the Nord Pool price are unobserved, the price is identical for all households within a grid area (P_{i,a,t} = P_{a,t}) and no logs of the price are taken, to avoid bias
a small constant is added to hourly consumption before taking logs, so that near-zero observations are not excluded
PSO (Public Service Obligation) charges are not taken into account (1-5 oere/kWh in 2020 and the first quarter of 2021, 0 thereafter)
the reduced consumption tax for electricity used to heat homes (above 4000 kWh per year) is not observed and not taken into account
the instrument is realized hourly wind energy production in MWh; expected wind production is unobserved
the average daily temperature is measured in Copenhagen and used as a proxy for weather conditions throughout the country
time dummies D_t cover hour of day, day of week, month of year and year
household-level standard errors are heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-robust (HAC) with automatic lag selection following Newey and West (1994)
Table 1 reports the first stage for the price averaged over five randomly selected households, because data security rules prohibit reporting estimates for a single household
registry characteristics are measured in 2020; the EV indicator comes from the 2022 vehicle register and includes plug-in hybrid cars
income and overall electricity consumption enter the demographic regressions as deciles
Table 3 uses Huber robust regression; Table A.3 uses probit

claims.statement: A DKK 1 increase in the hourly retail electricity price per kWh reduces hourly household electricity consumption by 2.6% on average (mean of the household-specific 2SLS semi-elasticities) among households in both grid areas pooled.

treatment.label: Hourly retail electricity price, P_{a,t} (DKK per kWh)

definition.value: The marginal price of one kWh of electricity for household i in grid area a at hour t, constructed as in Eq. (2.1): P = (1+tau)[E + G^T + G^D + T], i.e. the net electricity price (eltarif, a markup over the Nord Pool market price), the national transmission grid and system tariff, the local time-of-day distribution grid tariff and consumption taxes, all multiplied by VAT tau = 0.25. No logs of the price are taken because provider-specific markups are unobserved. Identical for all households within a grid area (P_{i,a,t} = P_{a,t}).

timing.value: The price of the same hour t in which consumption is measured; set on the Nord Pool market one day ahead and known to the consumer one day in advance

outcome.label: ln(C_{i,a,t}): log hourly electricity consumption of household i (kWh)

register_source.value: Danmarks Statistik (2024), Moduldata for elmaalere: hourly consumption of household i (C_{i,a,t})

definition.value: Hourly electricity consumption in kWh of household i recorded by its smart electricity meter, in natural logarithms; a small constant is added before taking logs so that near-zero observations are not dropped. Hourly observations from the start of 2020 until mid 2023.

timing.value: Hourly, contemporaneous with the price; start of 2020 until mid 2023

units.value: log points of hourly consumption (percent change) per DKK 1 per kWh increase in the hourly price

magnitude.interpretation: "a 1 DKK higher price leads to a mean (median) reduction of electricity consumption by 2.6% (2.1%)"; for this row the mean is -0.026 and the median -0.021 (robust mean -0.022, SD 0.055)

estimand.target_population: Households in both grid areas pooled for which a household-specific semi-elasticity could be estimated, after trimming the top and bottom 1% of estimates (N = 24395)
estimand.time_horizon: short run, hourly: the response of consumption in hour t to the price in hour t
estimand.formal_query: E[ln C | do(P = p+1)] - E[ln C | do(P = p)] for household i, averaged over households

population.description: Danish households with a smart electricity meter in the Radius grid area (Greater Copenhagen, price zone DK2) and the Trefor grid area (Jutland, DK1), present in the register micro-data between 2020 and 2023 at a unique household-address combination; a subset of almost 25,000 households.
population.region: Denmark: the Radius grid area (Greater Copenhagen, price zone DK2) and the Trefor grid area (Jutland, price zone DK1)
population.selection: Households present in the micro-data in every year 2020-2023; only unique household-address combinations; addresses with hourly consumption of exactly 0 kWh for a week or more excluded; addresses using more than 25 kWh within an hour for more than 1000 h excluded; top and bottom 1/75 of total consumption excluded; for computational reasons only a subsample of Radius and Trefor households is analysed; Table 2 trims the top and bottom 1% of the estimated elasticities.

identification.source_of_variation: Hourly variation in realized Danish wind power generation (MWh), largely driven by exogenous wind speed, conditional on year, month, day-of-week and hour-of-day dummies and the average daily temperature measured in Copenhagen.
identification.instrument: hourly wind power production W_t, measured in MWh

key_assumptions.assumption: Relevance: the instrument is sufficiently correlated with the hourly electricity price, Cov(W_t, P_{a,t}) != 0
key_assumptions.supported_by: First-stage results in Table 1; Kleibergen-Paap F-statistic of 134 (Radius) and 188 (Trefor)

implies_edges.from: W_t: hourly wind energy production (MWh)
implies_edges.to: P_{a,t}: hourly retail electricity price (DKK/kWh)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: wind energy production affects household electricity demand only through the retail price, Cov(W_t, nu_t) = 0
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion of curtailment, of severe weather events (addressed by time fixed effects and the average daily temperature) and of macroeconomic developments (addressed by annual fixed effects); the argument that much Danish wind power is produced offshore

implies_edges.from: W_t: hourly wind energy production (MWh)
implies_edges.to: ln(C_{i,a,t}): log hourly household electricity consumption

key_assumptions.assumption: Strict exogeneity: the instrument is uncorrelated with past, contemporaneous and future shocks to the demand equation, E(W_t nu_{t+j}) = 0 for all j
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argument that wind production is largely determined by stochastic weather conditions, primarily wind speed, and is therefore plausibly unaffected by short-run demand shocks

rhs: nu: shocks to the demand equation at all leads and lags (nu_{t+j})
given: D_t: hour-of-day, day-of-week, month-of-year and year dummies

implies_edges.from: nu: shocks to the demand equation at all leads and lags (nu_{t+j})
implies_edges.to: W_t: hourly wind energy production (MWh)

key_assumptions.assumption: Realized wind energy production is a good stand-in for the expected wind production that market participants price on
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assertion that expected and realized wind energy production are likely to be highly correlated (following Hirth et al., 2024)

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysed subsample of households is representative of the entire sample of households
key_assumptions.supported_by: A convergence analysis indicating that the sample size is sufficient for the estimated elasticity to converge to a constant value (results not reported)

implies_edges.from: S: inclusion in the analysed subsample (presence 2020-2023, unique address, consumption filters, 1% trimming)
implies_edges.to: ln(C_{i,a,t}): log hourly household electricity consumption

key_assumptions.assumption: The semi-elasticity beta_{1,i} is constant over the whole 2020 to mid-2023 period for a given household, and consumption responds to the price in the same hour

threats_discussed: simultaneity: expected residential demand affects the price set on the market, and short-term load forecasting by retailers makes the endogeneity persist even though prices are set one day ahead
wind energy curtailment could generate reverse causality from low demand to low wind production
severe weather events (cold temperatures, high wind speeds) could raise heating demand and wind production at the same time, violating the exclusion restriction
macroeconomic developments could affect both electricity demand and wind capacity installation in the medium to long run
expected rather than realized wind energy production is what market participants price on, and expected production is unobserved
fixed-price contracts, which are not observed, insulate some households from hourly price fluctuations
random measurement noise in the household-level estimates can push estimated elasticities away from the true value
robustness_checks: separate estimation and reporting by grid area (Radius and Trefor)
trimming the top and bottom 1% of the estimated semi-elasticities
a convergence analysis to check that the household subsample is large enough for the estimated elasticity to converge
HAC (Newey-West) standard errors with automatic lag selection per household
Kleibergen-Paap F-statistics of 134 (Radius) and 188 (Trefor) for instrument strength
conversion of the semi-elasticity into a dimensionless price elasticity for comparison with Hirth et al. (2024), Fabra et al. (2021) and Knaut and Paulus (2016)
Table A.3: probit regressions for the indicator of a significantly negative elasticity, alongside the Huber robust regressions of Table 3
unresolved_confounders: provider-specific markups over the Nord Pool market price are not observed, so the constructed price misses them
the reduced consumption tax applying when electricity is used for home heating (above 4000 kWh per year) is not observed
the household's contract type (hourly versus fixed price) is not observed, and fixed-price households may dampen the measured response
the electricity provider selected by the household is not observed

estimator.value: 2SLS instrumental variables, run separately for each household on that household's own hourly time series (Eqs. 3.3-3.4), with heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-robust (HAC) standard errors and automatic lag selection (Newey and West, 1994); Table 2 reports summary statistics of the household-level estimates after trimming the top and bottom 1%.

estimation.specification: Eqs. (3.3) and (3.4): first stage regresses the hourly price P_{a,t} on wind energy production W_t, time dummies D_t (hour of day, day of week, month of year, year) and the average daily temperature T_{a,t}; the second stage regresses ln(C_{i,a,t}) on the predicted price, D_t and T_{a,t}, separately for each household.
controls: average daily temperature measured in Copenhagen (proxy for weather conditions)
estimation.clustering: no clustering; heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-robust (HAC) standard errors with automatic lag selection per household

value.as_printed: ln(C_{i,a,t}) = beta_{0,i} + beta_{1,i} Phat_{a,t} + beta_{2,i} D_t + beta_{3,i} T_{a,t} + v_{t,i}
value.parameter_of_interest: beta_{1,i} = sigma-tilde_i, the semi-price elasticity for household i
value.normalisation: The price enters in levels (DKK/kWh) rather than logs, because provider markups are unobserved; a small constant is added to consumption before taking logs; D_t are dummies, so one hour of day, day of week, month of year and year is the omitted base category.

value.claimed_domain: Short-run hourly residential electricity demand in Denmark; the authors argue the analysed subsample is representative for the entire sample of households.
boundary_conditions: only the overall hourly demand response; which behavioural adjustment (intertemporal shifting versus lower total use) drives it is explicitly beyond the paper's scope
short-run responses only; long-run responses involving investments or habit changes are not covered
households facing hourly retail prices; households on fixed-price contracts are insulated from short-term price fluctuations

theory_referenced: the microeconomic law of demand for ordinary goods
rational inattention (Gabaix, 2014; Sims, 2003)

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: In contrast to our findings, Fabra et al. (2021) document that Spanish consumers do not adjust consumption in response to price signals.

Our estimate is somewhat larger than the estimates by Hirth et al. (2024), possibly reflecting the use of household-specific data as well as the different retail market structure in Denmark, compared to Germany.
Our estimates are within the range reported in Knaut and Paulus (2016).

outcomes_examined_not_reported: first-stage estimates for an individual randomly selected household from each grid area: not reportable under the data security rules, so Table 1 reports the first stage for the price averaged over five random households
the convergence analysis of the household sample size (described but not reported)
ambiguities: Table 2 reports no standard error or test for the mean semi-elasticity, so statistically_significant is left null for this row; significance is reported only household by household (29% significantly below zero at the 90% level).

The last two columns of Table 2 are headed '>0' and '<0' with 69% and 31%, while the text on p. 7 says 69% of households have a negative and 31% a positive elasticity; the column headings appear to be swapped relative to the text.
N is printed as '24.395' / '12.609' / '11.786' with a point as thousands separator; transcribed as 24395 / 12609 / 11786 counts of households.

estimator.value: 2SLS instrumental variables, run separately for each household on that household's own hourly time series (Eqs. 3.3-3.4), with heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-robust (HAC) standard errors and automatic lag selection (Newey and West, 1994); Table 2 reports summary statistics of the household-level estimates after trimming the top and bottom 1%. The dimensionless elasticity is obtained by scaling the mean semi-elasticity by the average price, following Hirth et al. (2024).

estimation.specification: Eqs. (3.3) and (3.4): first stage regresses the hourly price P_{a,t} on wind energy production W_t, time dummies D_t (hour of day, day of week, month of year, year) and the average daily temperature T_{a,t}; the second stage regresses ln(C_{i,a,t}) on the predicted price, D_t and T_{a,t}, separately for each household. The reported elasticity rescales beta_{1,i} by the average price level, as in Eq. (3.2).
controls: average daily temperature measured in Copenhagen (proxy for weather conditions)

anchor_quote.text: We find that older, more educated households with a high relative electricity consumption but lower relative income are significantly more likely to reduce demand if prices are higher.

claims.statement: In the probit regression for whether a household's estimated semi-price elasticity is negative and significant at the 10% level (Table A.3, column (3)), an average age of adult household members of 75 and older (rather than below 35) carries a coefficient of 0.384, i.e. a higher probability of being price responsive (a significantly negative semi-elasticity).

register_source.value: Danish registry data for the year 2020: the average age of adult household members (no register code or variable name given)

definition.value: Indicator equal to one if the average age of adult household members falls in the band 75 and older; households below 35 are the omitted age group. The average age is taken from the registry data for the year 2020.

timing.value: Measured in the registry data for the year 2020 (electric-vehicle ownership in the 2022 vehicle register), while the semi-elasticity it is matched to is estimated over 2020 to mid 2023

timing.value: Based on the semi-elasticity estimated over the whole 2020 to mid-2023 period; characteristics measured in 2020 (EV ownership in 2022)

units.value: probit index coefficient (not a marginal effect) for the probability that the household's estimated semi-elasticity is negative and significant at the 10% level, relative to households whose adult members are on average below 35

magnitude.interpretation: "Fourthly, there seems to be an inverse u-shaped relation between age and the elasticity. population.description: Households in the Radius (Greater Copenhagen) and Trefor (Jutland) grid areas with an estimated household-specific semi-price elasticity that can be matched to the Danish administrative registry variables used in Table A.3 column (3); N = 23664.

population.selection: Households present in the micro-data in every year 2020-2023; only unique household-address combinations; addresses with hourly consumption of exactly 0 kWh for a week or more excluded; addresses using more than 25 kWh within an hour for more than 1000 h excluded; top and bottom 1/75 of total consumption excluded; for computational reasons only a subsample of Radius and Trefor households is analysed; Table 2 trims the top and bottom 1% of the estimated elasticities. households on fixed-price contracts, whose demand is unaffected by marginal price signals, are mixed in with truly price-responsive households
